system_overview: This specification models Lamport's bakery algorithm, a mutual exclusion protocol that allows N concurrent processes to coordinate access to a critical section without relying on atomic hardware operations. The algorithm is named after the analogy of customers taking numbered tickets at a bakery and waiting for their turn to be served. It was originally published by Leslie Lamport in 1974 as 'A New Solution of Dijkstra's Concurrent Programming Problem'.
actors_and_components: The system consists of N processes (numbered 1 through N) that repeatedly cycle between a non-critical section, a doorway (entry protocol), a critical section, and an exit protocol. Each process independently competes for exclusive access to the critical section.
state_variables: The system tracks two shared arrays indexed by process identifier: (1) a ticket number for each process, representing its position in the queue (zero means the process is not competing), and (2) a boolean flag for each process indicating whether it is currently in the doorway choosing its ticket number. Each process also maintains local state for iterating over other processes during the entry protocol, tracking the maximum ticket number seen so far, and identifying which process is currently being checked in the waiting loop.
initial_state: All ticket numbers are zero (no process is competing). All choosing flags are false (no process is in the doorway). Each process starts in its non-critical section.
actions: The algorithm proceeds in phases for each process: (1) Entry/doorway: The process sets its choosing flag to true, scans all other processes' ticket numbers to find the current maximum, selects a ticket number strictly greater than that maximum, then sets its choosing flag to false. (2) Waiting: The process iterates over every other process and, for each one, first waits until that process is not currently choosing a ticket number, then waits until either that process has a ticket number of zero (not competing) or the current process has higher priority. Priority is determined by lexicographic comparison of (ticket number, process identifier) pairs — a lower ticket number wins, and ties are broken by lower process identifier. (3) Critical section: The process executes its critical section. (4) Exit: The process resets its ticket number to zero and returns to the non-critical section. Nondeterminism is present in the entry and exit steps — the flag and ticket number may be written multiple times (with arbitrary intermediate values) before settling on their intended values, modeling the fact that these writes are not assumed to be atomic.
safety_properties: Mutual exclusion: no two distinct processes may be in the critical section at the same time.
liveness_properties: Deadlock freedom: if any process is trying to enter the critical section, then eventually some process enters the critical section. Starvation freedom: every process that begins trying to enter the critical section will eventually enter it.
model_bounds: The number of processes N is declared as a constant natural number. For model checking, N must be instantiated with a specific finite value (commonly 2 or 3).
additional_assumptions: Weak fairness is assumed for each process when it is not in its non-critical section — that is, if a process is trying to make progress (it is past the non-critical section), it will eventually take a step. The algorithm models non-atomic reads and writes by allowing nondeterministic stuttering at the entry and exit points, where variables may be assigned intermediate arbitrary values before reaching their intended values. A formal machine-checked proof of mutual exclusion is included in the specification.
